title: FAR U3·W2 — Governmental Accounting (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — a different rulebook entirely

Governmental accounting is its own FAR world: a different standard-setter (GASB, not FASB), fund accounting, and a measurement basis that does not exist in business accounting. MBG itself is a private company, but state and local governments are major construction clients, so understanding how a municipality accounts for the project it hires MBG to build is genuinely useful — and it is heavily tested.

Fund accounting and the standard-setter

The Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) sets standards for state and local governments. Governments account through funds — self-balancing sets of accounts for specific activities — grouped into three categories:

  • Governmental funds: general, special revenue, capital projects, debt service, and permanent funds.
  • Proprietary funds: enterprise (services to the public for a fee, e.g., a water utility) and internal service funds.
  • Fiduciary funds: custodial and trust funds held for others.

Two measurement focuses and bases

This is the heart of the topic:

  • Governmental funds use the current financial resources measurement focus and the modified accrual basis. They report fund balance, not net position, and record expenditures (not expenses).
  • Proprietary and fiduciary funds, and the government-wide statements, use the economic resources focus and full accrual basis — like a business.

Under modified accrual, revenue is recognized when it is measurable and available (collectible within the period or soon enough after — commonly within 60 days — to pay current liabilities), and expenditures are recognized when the related liability is incurred. So a long-lived asset purchase is an expenditure in full when acquired in a governmental fund, with no depreciation in that fund.

Government-wide versus fund statements

A government presents both government-wide statements (full accrual, economic resources, all activities together except fiduciary) and fund financial statements (governmental funds on modified accrual). A reconciliation bridges the two — for example, adding back capital assets and long-term debt that the fund statements do not carry. Encumbrance accounting reserves budgetary resources when a purchase order is issued, a budgetary control unique to governments.

The five governmental fund types

Within the governmental category each fund has a job. The General Fund accounts for all resources not required to be in another fund — the main operating fund. Special revenue funds account for revenues legally restricted to specific purposes (a gas-tax fund for road maintenance). Capital projects funds account for resources used to acquire or build major capital assets (the school a municipality hires a contractor to construct). Debt service funds accumulate resources to pay principal and interest on general long-term debt. Permanent funds report resources legally restricted so that only earnings, not principal, may be spent (a cemetery-care endowment). The capital assets built through a capital projects fund and the bonds that financed them do not sit in the fund — they appear only in the government-wide statements.

Fund balance classifications

GASB 54 sorts governmental-fund fund balance into a hierarchy reflecting how constrained the resources are: nonspendable (not in spendable form — inventory, prepaids, the principal of a permanent fund), restricted (constrained by external parties or law), committed (constrained by the government’s highest decision-making authority), assigned (intended for a purpose but not formally committed), and unassigned (the residual, found mainly in the General Fund). The classification communicates spending constraints to users and is a reliable exam item — distinguishing committed (formal action) from assigned (mere intent) in particular.

Nonexchange revenue recognition

Governments earn much revenue without an exchange, and GASB sorts these into four classes. Derived tax revenues (sales and income taxes) are recognized when the underlying transaction occurs. Imposed nonexchange revenues (property taxes, fines) are recognized in the period for which they are levied — property tax is recorded when an enforceable legal claim arises and recognized for the budget year it funds. Government-mandated and voluntary nonexchange transactions (grants) are recognized when all eligibility requirements are met. On modified accrual the additional available criterion still applies — revenue measurable but not yet available is deferred as a liability.

Budgetary accounting and encumbrances

Governments record their legally adopted budget in the accounts. The opening budgetary entry debits Estimated revenues, credits Appropriations (the spending authority), and books the difference to budgetary fund balance. During the year, issuing a purchase order records an encumbrance — debit Encumbrances, credit budgetary fund balance reserved for encumbrances — reserving appropriation so the government cannot overspend. When the goods arrive, the encumbrance is reversed and the actual expenditure and liability are recorded. Encumbrances are not expenditures and not GAAP-basis expenses; they are a budgetary control, and any outstanding at year-end are disclosed as commitments.

The government-wide statements and net position

The two government-wide statements use full accrual. The Statement of Net Position reports all assets and deferred outflows less liabilities and deferred inflows, with the residual net position split into net investment in capital assets, restricted, and unrestricted. The Statement of Activities uses a distinctive net-(expense)/revenue format: each function’s direct expenses are reduced by its program revenues (charges for services, operating and capital grants) to show the net cost borne by taxpayers, with general revenues (taxes) reported below. Fiduciary activities are excluded from the government-wide statements because the resources are not the government’s to use.

Reconciliation and the reporting package

Because the fund statements (modified accrual) and government-wide statements (full accrual) differ, a reconciliation bridges them: it adds back the capital assets (net of accumulated depreciation) and the long-term debt that governmental funds do not report, and converts capital-outlay and debt-principal expenditures back to the accrual measures. The full annual report — the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) — wraps the basic statements with Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) and other required supplementary information (RSI) such as the budgetary comparison schedule. Proprietary funds add a statement of cash flows with four categories (operating, noncapital financing, capital and related financing, and investing) — note the two financing categories, unlike the single financing section in business accounting.

Interfund activity and capital project flows

Resources move between funds, and the labels matter. Interfund transfers (the General Fund subsidizing a debt service fund) are reported as other financing sources/uses, not revenues or expenditures. Interfund loans create a due-to/due-from and are not revenue at all. When a city issues bonds in a capital projects fund to build a school, the proceeds are an other financing source — the fund records no long-term liability, since that debt appears only government-wide — and the construction payments to the contractor are expenditures as incurred. The matching debt service fund later records principal and interest as expenditures only when due and payable, not as they accrue — another modified-accrual hallmark. Special items and significant one-time flows, when present, are reported separately below the normal revenues and expenditures so users can see them distinctly.

CMA bridge

CMA taught accrual job-cost accounting for a private builder; governmental accounting flips several assumptions — modified accrual, expenditures instead of expenses, and no depreciation in governmental funds. Recognizing where business GAAP does and does not apply is the exam skill.

Practice and recap

  1. Know GASB sets state/local government standards and the three fund categories.
  2. Governmental funds: current financial resources + modified accrual + expenditures.
  3. Proprietary/fiduciary and government-wide: economic resources + full accrual.
  4. Modified-accrual revenue = measurable and available; reconcile fund to government-wide statements.

Recap: governments use fund accounting under GASB; governmental funds run on modified accrual (revenue when measurable and available, expenditures when incurred, no depreciation) while proprietary funds and the government-wide statements use full accrual.

flashcards.front: Who sets state and local government accounting standards?
Governmental funds — measurement focus and basis
flashcards.back: Current financial resources focus; modified accrual basis (records expenditures).

flashcards.front: Proprietary/fiduciary and government-wide — focus and basis
flashcards.back: Economic resources focus; full accrual basis.
When measurable AND available (collectible within ~60 days to pay current liabilities).
Governmental, proprietary (enterprise, internal service), and fiduciary.

flashcards.front: Is there depreciation in governmental funds?
flashcards.back: No — capital outlays are expenditures in full when acquired; depreciation appears only in government-wide/proprietary statements.
Governmental funds record expenditures (modified accrual); accrual statements record expenses.
A budgetary reservation of resources when a purchase order/commitment is issued.

questions.q: Standards for state and local governments are set by:
questions.explain: GASB sets state and local governmental accounting standards.

questions.q: Governmental funds use which measurement focus and basis?
questions.explain: Governmental funds use the current financial resources focus and modified accrual basis.

questions.q: Under modified accrual, revenue is recognized when it is:
questions.explain: Modified accrual recognizes revenue when measurable and available.

questions.q: A water utility operated by a city is accounted for in which fund type?
questions.explain: A fee-for-service public utility is an enterprise (proprietary) fund using full accrual.

questions.q: In a governmental fund, the purchase of a fire truck is recorded as:
choices: An expenditure in full when acquired
questions.explain: Governmental funds record capital outlays as expenditures; no depreciation in the fund.

questions.q: Government-wide financial statements are prepared on the:
questions.explain: Government-wide statements use full accrual and the economic resources focus.

questions.q: Reserving budgetary resources when a purchase order is issued is called:
questions.explain: Encumbrance accounting reserves resources for outstanding commitments.
